trace.msg: Let's look at this puzzle carefully. I'll only move when I can explain why.

Going to (7,2,2), the next 4 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (2,2,1); going to (6,1,2), the next 3 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (2,2,1). So the line goes to (4,2,1).
Going to (4,1,2) would leave number 2 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going to (4,4,1) would leave number 2 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (2,2,1).
Number 2 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going to (1,4,2), every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves. So the line goes to (1,2,4).
Going to (2,1,4) would force the line onto number 20 before its turn; going to (1,2,6) would leave number 3 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (1,4,4).
Going to (1,6,4) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order). So the line goes to (1,4,2).
Number 4 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going to (2,6,1), the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at number 5. So the line goes to (4,4,1).
Number 5 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
I can't rule out to (2,6,1) or to (4,7,2) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (2,6,1).
I can't rule out to (1,6,2) or to (2,7,2) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (1,6,2).
I can't rule out to (2,7,4) or to (4,7,6) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (2,7,4).

Contradiction! Every way forward fails: going to (7,6,2) leaves no safe move afterwards; going to (6,7,4), every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves; going to (6,6,1) would force the line onto number 17 before its turn. So my guess (to (2,7,4) from cell (2,7,6)) was wrong, so the line must go to (4,7,6).

Contradiction! Going to (4,7,4) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order), and that's the only legal move. So my guess (to (1,6,2) from cell (2,6,1)) was wrong, so the line must go to (2,7,2).
Going to (4,7,2) would strand number 6: it would be left with only one free neighbour. So the line goes to (1,6,2).
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (1,6,4).
Going to (2,7,6) would force the line onto number 8 before its turn; going to (2,6,7), the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at cell (2,4,7). So the line goes to (1,4,6).
Going to (1,2,6) would leave number 8 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (2,4,7).
The line must go to (2,6,7): to (2,2,7) is number 21, which comes later; to (4,4,7) is number 13, which comes later.
Going to (4,7,6) would strand number 8: it would be left with only one free neighbour. So the line goes to (2,7,4).
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (4,7,4).
Cell (4,7,2) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (6,7,2).
Going to (6,6,1) would force the line onto number 17 before its turn; going to (7,6,2) leaves no safe move afterwards. So the line goes to (6,7,4).
Number 10 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Cell (4,7,6) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (4,6,7).
Going to (7,6,6), every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves. So the line goes to (6,4,7).

Going to (7,4,6) would strand number 13: it would be left with only one free neighbour; going to (6,2,7) would strand number 13: it would be left with only one free neighbour. So the line goes to (4,4,7).
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (4,2,7).
Going to (6,2,7), the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at cell (6,1,6). So the line goes to (4,1,6).
Going to (2,1,6) would cut off a group of 2 cells. So the line goes to (6,1,6).

Cell (6,6,1) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (6,4,1).
